arguments.name: Eternal life with temporal effects and direct presence
premises: An absolutely perfect being possesses its life completely without succession.
Knowing/willing/awareness need not all inherit the temporal processes of human cognition.
A relation across eternal and temporal modes can preserve their difference while permitting direct causal and cognitive presence.
bridge_principles: Temporal location of an effect need not be temporal location of the agent’s act.
ET′ direct-capacity clauses can be instantiated; the space/time analogy is relevant enough to challenge shared-mode objections.
arguments.conclusion: If those premises and bridges hold, an eternal agent can be cognitively/causally related to temporal persons without itself undergoing their succession.
arguments.strongest_objection: Lewis1984P/causal actuality and1988existential-presence/tense arguments challenge whether the proposed relation can be actual or coherent, rather than merely named.
arguments.strongest_reply: S&K1992argue against shared-mode requirements via nonspatial divine presence and make causal/awareness capacity explicit inET′.
unresolved_issues: Joint satisfiability of the capacity clauses
Independent grounds for perfect being and immaterial mind
Human constitution and persistence not supplied

arguments.name: The presentness objection and the exact later reply
arguments.position: Serious critic/reply assessment with version boundaries
premises: Lewis1984allows calendar knowledge but treats present actuality as an objective additional feature.
Lewis1988interprets classical existential presence as making all times ontologically equal.
An omniscient timeless being cannot omit an objective feature of reality.
bridge_principles: Direct presence across modes must be existential rather than merely representational.
The critic’s objective-tense or ontological-parity account is correct.
arguments.conclusion: Under those premises the1981account either misses present actuality or commits to a tenseless ontology; the selected1992reply contests cross-mode premises but does not conclusively settle the tense dispute.
arguments.strongest_objection: Defenders can challenge the necessity of shared mode and reject the critic’s assumed temporal-to-eternal transfer; temporalism is not established merely by insisting on it.
arguments.strongest_reply: Lewis’s strongest1988case appeals to the metaphysical price of spatial analogies; S&Kacknowledge the absolute-present mismatch. Its additional moral argument is now separately examined as Lewis1986→Oaklander1987–88 in A-P2T12-004.
unresolved_issues: The separate1986moral argument has an inspected Oaklander reply; its premises and broader identity adequacy remain disputed
Other named critics inspected only through1992attribution

arguments.name: Eternal relation does not entail human survival or identity
premises: ET/ET′relate an eternal entity and a temporal entity without identifying them.
An object being known or sustained does not specify its numerical identity across later episodes.
A finite history may be represented or present to another subject without further human experience beyond that history.
bridge_principles: Survival requires actual further subjectivity and a justified same-person relation, not only an eternal record or knower.
arguments.conclusion: The selected exchange cannot by itself establish enduring human consciousness, postmortem survival or a solution to branching/continuity; divine personhood and human identity remain distinct.
arguments.strongest_objection: A broader dualist, resurrection or constitution theory might add a same-bearer relation and a reason to expect continued experience.
arguments.strongest_reply: That would require its own defended premises and exact source evidence. P2T02was accepted only as a bounded derivative comparator and does not supply automatic survival.
unresolved_issues: The added Lewis/Oaklander exchange supplies identity analyses but no empirical identification or postmortem continuation evidence

arguments.name: Tenseless human persons, persistence and responsibility
arguments.position: Developed human-identity objection and actual direct reply
premises: Lewis treats moral responsibility and temporally extended action as requiring a persisting agent.
Lewis claims tenselessness permits only a temporal whole and its stages, and denies either can act or bear responsibility.
Oaklander denies the asserted ontology is necessary and distinguishes whole-person identity, indexed properties and continuity analyses from stage identity.
bridge_principles: Lewis’s conclusion requires his denial of a conscious, intending and responsible whole and his substantialist reading of persistence.
Oaklander’s reply requires at least one defended account of persisting agency that does not import the disputed substantialist or tensed premises.
arguments.conclusion: The claimed necessary incompatibility of tenselessness with human moral agency is contested by explicit alternatives; the exchange supplies no general evidential identity criterion, postmortem continuation or timeless human mentality.
arguments.strongest_objection: Lewis argues beyond stage nonidentity: a momentary stage cannot span an action, while a temporal whole allegedly has no consciousness, intentions or bodily members; a responsibility bearer must be more than a collection of events.
arguments.strongest_reply: Oaklander distinguishes tenseless continuants without parts, the whole referenced through different stages, and psychological/physical continuity; the ordinary sameness condition does not alone entail a simple substance. His reply attacks the claimed necessity rather than settling every metaphysical account.
unresolved_issues: Adequacy of indexed-property and token-reflexive analyses; Oaklander explicitly leaves tense debate open
Whether the whole/continuity accounts adequately explain consciousness and agency
Noncircular evidence, branching and interruption conditions not worked out
No identified postmortem subject or actual timeless ground
No actual later Lewis rebuttal established; Oaklander’s hypothetical rejoinder remains hypothetical
